subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 27-year-old man is the restrained driver in a head-on motor vehicle collision. He had eaten a large meal and drunk a liter of water shortly before the crash. He presents with hematuria, suprapubic pain, and difficulty voiding. CT cystography shows contrast extravasation into the peritoneal cavity.
question: Which of the following best explains this injury pattern?

options.text: Pelvic fracture with bony spicules perforating the anterior bladder wall
Direct blow to a full bladder causing dome rupture from abruptly increased intravesical pressure
Penetrating injury to the lower ureter with urine leakage
Straddle injury disrupting the bulbar (spongy) urethra
Shear injury at the bulbomembranous junction of the urethra

explanation_correct: The dome (superior wall) is the weakest part of the bladder. A direct blow (eg, seatbelt) to a full bladder abruptly raises intravesical pressure, rupturing the dome and releasing urine into the peritoneal cavity. Peritoneal absorption of urine can then raise BUN and creatinine, mimicking renal injury. This matches the intraperitoneal contrast extravasation.

explanation_incorrect.A: Pelvic fracture with bony spicules perforates the anterior bladder wall or neck and causes extraperitoneal (retropubic) urine, not intraperitoneal leakage.
explanation_incorrect.C: A ureteral injury would not produce suprapubic pain with intraperitoneal bladder contrast extravasation; the bladder wall is the source here.
explanation_incorrect.D: A straddle injury causes anterior urethral (bulbar) disruption with scrotal hematoma, not intraperitoneal urine.
explanation_incorrect.E: A bulbomembranous junction injury is a posterior urethral injury from pelvic fracture, producing a high-riding prostate and retropubic urine.

educationalObjective: Recognize that a blow to a full bladder ruptures the dome (weakest part), causing intraperitoneal urine and elevated BUN/creatinine from peritoneal absorption.

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 41-year-old woman sustains a pelvic fracture in a motor vehicle collision. She has hematuria and suprapubic tenderness. Imaging shows urine confined to the retropubic (extraperitoneal) space, with no free intraperitoneal fluid. A bony fragment is seen adjacent to the bladder neck.
question: Which of the following mechanisms best accounts for this pattern of bladder injury?

options.text: Abrupt increase in intravesical pressure against a distended dome
Direct penetrating trauma to the bladder dome
Isolated lower rib fracture with an associated renal laceration
Perforation of the anterior bladder wall or neck by bony spicules from the pelvic fracture
Deceleration shearing of the renal pedicle

explanation_correct: Pelvic fractures can displace bony spicules that perforate the anterior bladder wall or bladder neck. Because this portion of the bladder is covered only extraperitoneally, urine accumulates in the retropubic space rather than the peritoneal cavity. This is the classic extraperitoneal bladder injury, in contrast to dome rupture from a full bladder, which is intraperitoneal.

explanation_incorrect.A: An abrupt rise in intravesical pressure in a distended bladder ruptures the dome (weakest part) and causes intraperitoneal urine, not a confined retropubic collection.
explanation_incorrect.B: Direct penetrating trauma to the dome would produce intraperitoneal leakage, not urine limited to the retropubic space.
explanation_incorrect.C: Lower rib fractures are associated with renal injury (flank bruising, pain, hematuria), not bladder neck perforation by bony spicules.
explanation_incorrect.E: Renal pedicle shear from deceleration causes a renal vascular injury with hematuria and flank pain, not bladder injury with retropubic urine.

educationalObjective: Contrast extraperitoneal bladder injury (pelvic fracture, bony spicules, retropubic urine) with intraperitoneal dome rupture from a full bladder.

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 35-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a perineal straddle injury. He has blood at the urethral meatus, hematuria, and difficulty voiding. The resident prepares to insert a Foley catheter before any further imaging.
question: Which of the following is relatively contraindicated in this clinical setting?

options.text: Urethral catheterization
Retrograde urethrography
Vital sign monitoring
Analgesia
Perineal examination

explanation_correct: Urethral injury is suggested by blood at the meatus, hematuria, and difficulty voiding, and it occurs almost exclusively in males. Urethral catheterization is relatively contraindicated because it can worsen the injury or create a false passage; further evaluation (eg, retrograde urethrography) should come first.

explanation_incorrect.B: Retrograde urethrography is the appropriate diagnostic study to evaluate a suspected urethral injury, not a contraindication.
explanation_incorrect.C: Vital sign monitoring is standard trauma care and is not contraindicated.
explanation_incorrect.D: Analgesia is appropriate and helpful; it does not worsen a urethral injury.
explanation_incorrect.E: A careful perineal examination is part of the trauma evaluation and is not contraindicated.

educationalObjective: Recall that suspected urethral injury (blood at meatus, hematuria, difficulty voiding) makes catheterization relatively contraindicated.

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 28-year-old man falls astride a fence rail while bicycling. He develops pain and swelling in the perineum and notes blood at the urethral meatus. Over the next hour, the scrotum becomes markedly swollen and ecchymotic.
question: The injury most likely involves disruption of which of the following?

options.text: Prostatic urethra
Bulbomembranous junction
Bulbar (spongy) urethra
Renal pelvis
Bladder dome

explanation_correct: A perineal straddle injury compresses the bulbar (spongy) urethra against the pubic symphysis, disrupting it. Blood and urine can dissect into the scrotum, producing a scrotal hematoma. If Buck fascia is torn, urine escapes into the perineal space. This is the classic anterior urethral injury.

explanation_incorrect.A: The prostatic urethra is not the site of a straddle injury; it is involved in posterior injuries associated with pelvic fracture or prostatic disease.
explanation_incorrect.B: The bulbomembranous junction is the weakest point of the posterior urethra and is disrupted by pelvic fractures with a high-riding prostate, not by a straddle injury.
explanation_incorrect.D: The renal pelvis is not involved in a perineal straddle injury; renal injury presents with flank pain and hematuria.
explanation_incorrect.E: The bladder dome ruptures from a direct blow to a full bladder with increased intravesical pressure, causing intraperitoneal urine, not a straddle injury.

educationalObjective: Associate straddle injuries with anterior (bulbar/spongy) urethral disruption, scrotal hematoma, and Buck fascia involvement.

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 33-year-old man is involved in a motor vehicle collision and sustains a pelvic fracture. He has blood at the urethral meatus and cannot void. On rectal examination, the prostate is displaced superiorly and is difficult to appreciate.
question: Which of the following best explains these findings?

options.text: Anterior urethral injury at the bulbar urethra from a straddle mechanism
Bladder dome rupture with intraperitoneal urine
Renal artery thrombosis from deceleration
Perforation of the anterior bladder wall by bony spicules
Posterior urethral disruption at the bulbomembranous junction

explanation_correct: Pelvic fracture can disrupt the posterior urethra at the bulbomembranous junction, its weakest point. Urine leaks into the retropubic space, and the prostate becomes displaced superiorly — a 'high-riding' prostate on rectal examination. Together with blood at the meatus and inability to void, this is classic for posterior urethral injury.

explanation_incorrect.A: A bulbar urethral injury is an anterior urethral injury from a straddle, producing a scrotal hematoma rather than a high-riding prostate.
explanation_incorrect.B: Bladder dome rupture causes intraperitoneal urine and elevated BUN/creatinine, not a high-riding prostate or blood at the meatus.
explanation_incorrect.C: Renal artery thrombosis would cause flank pain and hematuria without urethral bleeding or a displaced prostate.
explanation_incorrect.D: Anterior bladder wall perforation by bony spicules causes extraperitoneal (retropubic) urine but is a bladder injury, not the urethral disruption that produces meatal blood and a high-riding prostate.

educationalObjective: Associate pelvic fracture with posterior urethral disruption at the bulbomembranous junction: blood at meatus, retropubic urine, and a high-riding prostate.

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 45-year-old man is struck in the flank during an altercation. He develops bruising over the lower ribs, left flank pain, and hematuria. He is hemodynamically stable.
question: Which of the following injuries is most consistent with this presentation?

options.text: Bladder dome rupture
Renal injury from a direct blow or lower rib fracture
Posterior urethral disruption
Bulbar urethral disruption
Penile fracture

explanation_correct: Renal injury typically follows blunt trauma such as a direct blow or lower rib fracture. It presents with bruising, flank pain, and hematuria. The mechanism and findings here — flank bruising, pain, and hematuria after a blow — are classic for renal injury.

explanation_incorrect.A: Bladder dome rupture follows a blow to a full bladder and produces suprapubic pain and intraperitoneal urine, not flank bruising.
explanation_incorrect.C: Posterior urethral disruption results from pelvic fracture with blood at the meatus and a high-riding prostate, not isolated flank trauma.
explanation_incorrect.D: Bulbar urethral disruption is caused by a perineal straddle injury with scrotal hematoma and meatal blood.
explanation_incorrect.E: Penile fracture is a rupture of the corpus cavernosum during erection with a 'snapping' sound and penile swelling, not flank pain and hematuria.

educationalObjective: Recognize renal injury from blunt flank trauma or lower rib fracture by the triad of bruising, flank pain, and hematuria.
